claims.text: The conventional eutectic HEA has a multiphase microstructure comprising a ductile matrix and an intermetallic phase.
The coexisting phases have distinctly different electrochemical potentials.
Compositional and electrochemical disparities cause phase boundaries to act as galvanic couples.
Potential differences between the phases create localized galvanic cells at phase boundaries.
Mechanical wear repeatedly exposes fresh dissimilar phase interfaces.
Repeated exposure of fresh interfaces keeps galvanically reactive sites active.
Sustained galvanic activity accelerates localized corrosion.
Accelerated localized corrosion increases overall coupled degradation.
Localized galvanic corrosion at phase boundaries is the primary driver of accelerated coupled wear–corrosion degradation at elevated temperature.
Tailored annealing homogenizes phase composition and minimizes electrochemical disparities between phases.
The conventionally processed alloy will have a markedly higher total degradation rate than the homogenized annealed baseline.
The conventionally processed alloy will have a significantly larger corrosion component because of enhanced galvanic activity at phase boundaries.
The conventionally processed alloy may have a modestly higher wear rate as a secondary consequence of accelerated corrosion.
The proposed mechanism applies at 350–450 °C in a chloride-rich medium under controlled wear that repeatedly exposes phase interfaces.
The quantitative contribution of galvanic corrosion relative to mechanical wear is uncertain.
